## Trademarks

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Trademarks")]

Taco John's has adopted and trademarked the term "West-Mex" to describe their food and service attitude.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-Arellano_2013-33) The company defines "West-Mex" food as having fresh, bold flavors, including their [signature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signature_dish "Signature dish") "Potato Olés", sauces, spices, and salsas.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-The_State-2)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-34)

In 1989, the company trademarked the phrase "[Taco Tuesday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_Tuesday "Taco Tuesday")" in every U.S. state except New Jersey, where another restaurant had already trademarked it. As of 2023, Taco John's had abandoned its trademark on the phrase.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-35)

## Advertising, mascots, slogans, and logos

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Advertising, mascots, slogans, and logos")]

### Mascots

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Mascots")]

Taco John's early [mascot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mascot "Mascot"), depicted on their street signage above the words "The Hottest Spot In Town," was a devil character. Later mascots were versions of a cartoonish Mexican character named Juan with a giant [sombrero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sombrero "Sombrero") and a [donkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey "Donkey") named Pépé.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-36) That figure was replaced in the mid-1990s by a more modern, artistic image.

Taco John's recent advertising icons have included [Whiplash the Cowboy Monkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiplash_the_Cowboy_Monkey "Whiplash the Cowboy Monkey"), a popular rodeo attraction and PRCA Entertainer of the Year, who rides on his dog Ben to the rescue of hungry taco lovers.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-37)

Punk band In Defence performed their song "Call More Dudes" in a Taco John's as part of a tribute to the franchise.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-38)

In the 1990s, Taco John's slogan was "A Whole Lotta Mexican," which accompanied a jingle that stated "Once we getcha, then we gotcha.... gotcha coming back for more! Taco John's."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-39)

## Criticisms and controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Criticisms and controversies")]

### 2006 _E. coli_ outbreak

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2006 E. coli outbreak")]

In December 2006, a reported 50 people became sick and 18 people were hospitalized after eating at a Taco John's restaurant in Iowa. Shortly after that, [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota") health officials reported that an additional 27 people became ill after eating at Taco John's restaurants in [Rio Grande City, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Grande_City,_Texas "Rio Grande City, Texas"), and [Grand Forks, North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Forks,_North_Dakota "Grand Forks, North Dakota").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-40) On December 14, [Black Hawk County, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hawk_County,_Iowa "Black Hawk County, Iowa") health officials stated that [lettuce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lettuce "Lettuce") tainted with _[E. coli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escherichia\_coli "Escherichia coli")_ had been discovered in the supply chain. That same day, a Cedar Falls couple filed a lawsuit against Taco John's after their 9-year-old daughter was hospitalized for symptoms of _E. coli_.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-41) Taco John's dropped its produce supplier, Bix Produce of [Grand Forks, North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Forks,_North_Dakota "Grand Forks, North Dakota"), as a result of the outbreaks. After a thorough investigation by the Minnesota Department of Health and the FDA, Bix Produce was cleared of any wrongdoing in the matter. The source of the outbreak was traced back to the growing fields in California. This incident came about at the same time as an unrelated _E. coli_ outbreak at [Taco Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_Bell "Taco Bell") restaurants in the midwestern United States.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-42)

### 2014 nametag incident

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 2014 nametag incident")]

In June 2014, Tyler Brandt, a 16-year-old employee at a Taco John's in [Yankton, South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yankton,_South_Dakota "Yankton, South Dakota"), quit his job due to his supervisor's alleged use of [homophobic slurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homophobia "Homophobia"). Brandt said his supervisor pressured him to wear a nametag that identified him as "Gaytard", and used that term to address him in front of customers and other employees. According to the Yankton store's general manager, Brandt chose the nickname for himself, and wasn't forced to wear the nametag.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-Yankton_Daily-43)

In September 2014, the [ACLU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACLU "ACLU") assisted Brandt in filing a federal discrimination charge with the [Equal Employment Opportunity Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Equal_Employment_Opportunity_Commission "United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission"),[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-ACLU_News-44) alleging that Taco John's violated the South Dakota Human Rights Act.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-ACLU_Ohio-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-46) Taco John's addressed the incident on its Facebook page, writing that it shares the belief that discrimination is wrong, but clarifying that the franchisor does not control its franchisees' day-to-day operations or personnel decisions.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-47)

### 2023 Taco Bell lawsuit over "Taco Tuesday" trademark

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 2023 Taco Bell lawsuit over \"Taco Tuesday\" trademark")]

Main article: [Taco Tuesday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_Tuesday "Taco Tuesday")

Taco John's obtained a [trademark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trademark "Trademark") for the phrase "Taco Tuesday" in 1989.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:0-48) On May 16, 2023, [Taco Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_Bell "Taco Bell") filed a petition with the [United States Patent and Trademark Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Patent_and_Trademark_Office "United States Patent and Trademark Office") to cancel the trademark, claiming "Taco Tuesday" was a commonplace saying and legally unavailable for trademark.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:2-50)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:0-48) Taco Bell did not seek any damages from Taco John's.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:2-50)

Taco John's CEO Jim Creel responded, "I'd like to thank our worthy competitors at Taco Bell for reminding everyone that Taco Tuesday is best celebrated at Taco John's."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:2-50)

In July 2023, Taco John's abandoned its trademark for the phrase, making it available for anyone to use. Creel said, "Paying millions of dollars to lawyers to defend our mark just doesn't feel like the right thing to do."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-52)

**Taco John's International, Inc.** is an American [fast food restaurant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_food_restaurant "Fast food restaurant"). The chain serves [Mexican-inspired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuisine_of_Mexico##Mexican_food_outside_Mexico "Cuisine of Mexico")[fast food](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast-food "Fast-food") as well as the company's [signature dish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signature_dish "Signature dish"), Potato Olés, which are bite-sized deep-fried potato nuggets coated with a proprietary blend of seasonings.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-The_State-2) Since 2025, the company has been headquartered in [St. Louis Park, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Park,_Minnesota "St. Louis Park, Minnesota").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-3)

As of 2022, the restaurant chain had 380 restaurants in about 22 states,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-all-locations-1) primarily in the [Midwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwestern_United_States "Midwestern United States") and [Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_States "Mountain States") regions.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-4)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Early days

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early days")]

Taco John's started in 1968 as a trailer called Taco House, run by John Turner.

Turner was an officer in the [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") who served during the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War") and was an aspiring [entrepreneur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entrepreneurship "Entrepreneurship"); he was stationed at [FE Warren AFB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_E._Warren_Air_Force_Base "Francis E. Warren Air Force Base"). Initially, Turner wanted to find a physical location for a [taco stand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_stand "Taco stand"). He went to James Woodson to find a location to lease, and Woodson redirected him to Harold W. Holmes, who converted one of his campers into a 12x30 trailer in seven days.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:1-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-kingfm.com-6) This was popular at [Cheyenne Frontier Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne_Frontier_Days "Cheyenne Frontier Days").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-kingfm.com-6) By the end of the year, the first official taco stand opened on the corner of Carey Ave and W 24th St (not to be confused with the first brick-and-mortar location a block away), continuing under the Taco House brand.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-tacojohnsfranchise.com-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-Derdak_2004-8)

### Name change, franchising, and growth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Name change, franchising, and growth")]

Turner began the shift to a [franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franchising "Franchising") in 1969 by selling the franchise rights to Woodson and Holmes, who changed the name to Taco John's in honor of Turner and opened a franchise store under the Taco John's banner.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-9) They also launched Woodson-Holmes Enterprises, which gave Woodson the restaurant franchise rights, and the company name became Taco John's International, Inc. The new franchise location featured Taco John's original [mascot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mascot "Mascot"), a devil, and displayed the tagline "the hottest spot in town".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-tacojohnsfranchise.com-7)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-10) More locations opened in 1969, including the [Loveland, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loveland,_Colorado "Loveland, Colorado"), location on Lincoln Avenue.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-11)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Taco_Johns_Athens_OH_USA.JPG/250px-Taco_Johns_Athens_OH_USA.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taco_Johns_Athens_OH_USA.JPG)

Taco John's freestanding unit in [Athens, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens,_Ohio "Athens, Ohio"), with [Pizza Hut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pizza_Hut "Pizza Hut")

This led to more growth of the brand in the 1970s, with many new locations opening, including the 100th store in [Scottsbluff, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottsbluff,_Nebraska "Scottsbluff, Nebraska"), in 1975.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:3-12) In 1973, the first physical brick-and-mortar, in-the-ground Taco John's was built at Carey Ave and W 23rd St in Cheyenne, Wyoming, including a [drive-through](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drive-through "Drive-through"). The original Taco John's building was moved to S Greeley Hwy and I-80, where it was demolished, but there is still a Taco John's at that location today.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:1-5)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:3-12)

Due to large growth, Taco John's upgraded its Cheyenne headquarters in 1985. The [Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa "Iowa")-based franchise was the first to gain over $1 million in sales in 1994.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:3-12)

### Brand partnerships with some challenges

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Brand partnerships with some challenges")]

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/63/Goodtimes-TacoJohns.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Goodtimes-TacoJohns.JPG)

Good Times/Taco John's combination restaurant in [Commerce City, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commerce_City,_Colorado "Commerce City, Colorado"), replaced and now demolished for a Starbucks.

By 2004, Taco John's began a new form of expansion normally seen in larger brands, involving partnerships with other restaurants, including local brands like [Good Times Burgers & Frozen Custard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Times_Burgers_&_Frozen_Custard "Good Times Burgers & Frozen Custard") and [Steak Escape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steak_Escape "Steak Escape") in 2004[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-14) and an [Arby's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arby's "Arby's") in [Lindenhurst, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindenhurst,_New_York "Lindenhurst, New York"), that opened in 2015.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-15)

While some of these combo stores still exist, including the Taco John's/Steak Escape Combo at Logan St and E 58th Ave in [Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver "Denver"),[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-16) many have either embarked on a solo journey as the Cheyenne Taco John's did after Good Times disappeared around 2010,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-18) or even completely shuttered, as in [Commerce City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commerce_City,_Colorado "Commerce City, Colorado").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-20)

Around the same time that some of these combo restaurants were closing, the original franchise owners were reaching their final days. Woodson died at age 87 in 2008 in [Scottsdale, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottsdale,_Arizona "Scottsdale, Arizona").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-21) Holmes died in 2012 of heart complications at age 92 in a hospital in [Phoenix, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix,_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-22)

### Subsequent booms and challenges

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Subsequent booms and challenges")]

Although Taco John's targeted smaller [Midwestern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwestern_United_States "Midwestern United States") and [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_United_States "Western United States") communities in its early years, the chain also began expanding its presence in larger metropolitan areas like Denver and [Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_metropolitan_area "Kansas City metropolitan area"), where it had a minor presence since the 1980s.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-23) Taco John's also operates several outlets serving the U.S. Armed Forces through the [Army and Air Force Exchange Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_and_Air_Force_Exchange_Service "Army and Air Force Exchange Service") (AAFES).

While some Taco John's have closed, others have opened, and new experiments have arisen. For example, in 2016, Taco John's saw its first [Love's Travel Stop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love's "Love's") location open in [Liberal, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal,_Kansas "Liberal, Kansas").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-24) This was not the first instance of a Travel Stop combo, with one of the more recent Taco John's opening in the Loves Travel Center of [Berthoud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berthoud,_Colorado "Berthoud, Colorado") in 2018.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-25)

In April 2016, the company announced a deal to open 40 new stores in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)") and [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee"). The deal includes 20 stores in the [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") area and the Northeast with an option for 15 more.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-26) As of October 2016, the company had 390 restaurants spread throughout Wyoming and 24 other states.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-27) As of August 2021, there is only one New York location, in [JFK airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_International_Airport "John F. Kennedy International Airport").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-28)[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_]

In 2017, Taco John's opened 10 new locations and expanded to Tennessee and Indiana. In 2019, it planned to open new locations in central [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina") and [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-29)

As of August 2021, there are 380 locations,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-all-locations-1) with more planned.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-30)

In 2022, Taco John's filed suit against a small Minnesota restaurant chain, Taco Chon, which it accused of stealing its image and likeness.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-tacochon-31)

## Trademarks

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Trademarks")]

Taco John's has adopted and trademarked the term "West-Mex" to describe their food and service attitude.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-Arellano_2013-33) The company defines "West-Mex" food as having fresh, bold flavors, including their [signature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signature_dish "Signature dish") "Potato Olés", sauces, spices, and salsas.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-The_State-2)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-34)

In 1989, the company trademarked the phrase "[Taco Tuesday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_Tuesday "Taco Tuesday")" in every U.S. state except New Jersey, where another restaurant had already trademarked it. As of 2023, Taco John's had abandoned its trademark on the phrase.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-35)

## Advertising, mascots, slogans, and logos

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Advertising, mascots, slogans, and logos")]

### Mascots

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Mascots")]

Taco John's early [mascot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mascot "Mascot"), depicted on their street signage above the words "The Hottest Spot In Town," was a devil character. Later mascots were versions of a cartoonish Mexican character named Juan with a giant [sombrero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sombrero "Sombrero") and a [donkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey "Donkey") named Pépé.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-36) That figure was replaced in the mid-1990s by a more modern, artistic image.

Taco John's recent advertising icons have included [Whiplash the Cowboy Monkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiplash_the_Cowboy_Monkey "Whiplash the Cowboy Monkey"), a popular rodeo attraction and PRCA Entertainer of the Year, who rides on his dog Ben to the rescue of hungry taco lovers.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-37)

Punk band In Defence performed their song "Call More Dudes" in a Taco John's as part of a tribute to the franchise.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-38)

In the 1990s, Taco John's slogan was "A Whole Lotta Mexican," which accompanied a jingle that stated "Once we getcha, then we gotcha.... gotcha coming back for more! Taco John's."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-39)

## Criticisms and controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Criticisms and controversies")]

### 2006 _E. coli_ outbreak

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2006 E. coli outbreak")]

In December 2006, a reported 50 people became sick and 18 people were hospitalized after eating at a Taco John's restaurant in Iowa. Shortly after that, [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota") health officials reported that an additional 27 people became ill after eating at Taco John's restaurants in [Rio Grande City, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Grande_City,_Texas "Rio Grande City, Texas"), and [Grand Forks, North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Forks,_North_Dakota "Grand Forks, North Dakota").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-40) On December 14, [Black Hawk County, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hawk_County,_Iowa "Black Hawk County, Iowa") health officials stated that [lettuce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lettuce "Lettuce") tainted with _[E. coli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escherichia\_coli "Escherichia coli")_ had been discovered in the supply chain. That same day, a Cedar Falls couple filed a lawsuit against Taco John's after their 9-year-old daughter was hospitalized for symptoms of _E. coli_.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-41) Taco John's dropped its produce supplier, Bix Produce of [Grand Forks, North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Forks,_North_Dakota "Grand Forks, North Dakota"), as a result of the outbreaks. After a thorough investigation by the Minnesota Department of Health and the FDA, Bix Produce was cleared of any wrongdoing in the matter. The source of the outbreak was traced back to the growing fields in California. This incident came about at the same time as an unrelated _E. coli_ outbreak at [Taco Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_Bell "Taco Bell") restaurants in the midwestern United States.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-42)

### 2014 nametag incident

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 2014 nametag incident")]

In June 2014, Tyler Brandt, a 16-year-old employee at a Taco John's in [Yankton, South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yankton,_South_Dakota "Yankton, South Dakota"), quit his job due to his supervisor's alleged use of [homophobic slurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homophobia "Homophobia"). Brandt said his supervisor pressured him to wear a nametag that identified him as "Gaytard", and used that term to address him in front of customers and other employees. According to the Yankton store's general manager, Brandt chose the nickname for himself, and wasn't forced to wear the nametag.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-Yankton_Daily-43)

In September 2014, the [ACLU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACLU "ACLU") assisted Brandt in filing a federal discrimination charge with the [Equal Employment Opportunity Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Equal_Employment_Opportunity_Commission "United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission"),[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-ACLU_News-44) alleging that Taco John's violated the South Dakota Human Rights Act.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-ACLU_Ohio-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-46) Taco John's addressed the incident on its Facebook page, writing that it shares the belief that discrimination is wrong, but clarifying that the franchisor does not control its franchisees' day-to-day operations or personnel decisions.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-47)

### 2023 Taco Bell lawsuit over "Taco Tuesday" trademark

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taco_John%27s&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 2023 Taco Bell lawsuit over \"Taco Tuesday\" trademark")]

Main article: [Taco Tuesday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_Tuesday "Taco Tuesday")

Taco John's obtained a [trademark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trademark "Trademark") for the phrase "Taco Tuesday" in 1989.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:0-48) On May 16, 2023, [Taco Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_Bell "Taco Bell") filed a petition with the [United States Patent and Trademark Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Patent_and_Trademark_Office "United States Patent and Trademark Office") to cancel the trademark, claiming "Taco Tuesday" was a commonplace saying and legally unavailable for trademark.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:2-50)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:0-48) Taco Bell did not seek any damages from Taco John's.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:2-50)

Taco John's CEO Jim Creel responded, "I'd like to thank our worthy competitors at Taco Bell for reminding everyone that Taco Tuesday is best celebrated at Taco John's."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-:2-50)

In July 2023, Taco John's abandoned its trademark for the phrase, making it available for anyone to use. Creel said, "Paying millions of dollars to lawyers to defend our mark just doesn't feel like the right thing to do."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taco_John's#cite_note-52)

**John Napier Wyndham Turner** (June 7, 1929–September 19, 2020) was the 17th [prime minister of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_minister_of_Canada "Prime minister of Canada"), serving from June to September 1984. He served as [leader of the Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Liberal_Party_of_Canada "Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada") and [leader of the Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Official_Opposition_(Canada) "Leader of the Official Opposition (Canada)") from 1984 to 1990.

Turner practised law before being elected as a [member of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(Canada) "Member of Parliament (Canada)") (MP) in the [1962 federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_Canadian_federal_election "1962 Canadian federal election"). He served in the cabinet of Prime Minister [Pierre Trudeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau "Pierre Trudeau") as [minister of justice and attorney general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Justice_and_Attorney_General_of_Canada "Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada") from 1968 to 1972 and then as [minister of finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Finance_(Canada) "Minister of Finance (Canada)") from 1972 to 1975. As a cabinet minister, Turner came to be known as a leader of the [Business Liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Grit "Blue Grit") faction of the Liberal Party. Amid a global recession and the prospect of having to implement unpopular [wage and price controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wage_and_price_controls "Wage and price controls"), Turner resigned from his position in 1975.

From 1976 to 1984, Turner took a hiatus from politics, working as a corporate lawyer on [Bay Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Street "Bay Street"). Trudeau's resignation in 1984 triggered [a leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Liberal_Party_of_Canada_leadership_election "1984 Liberal Party of Canada leadership election"), which Turner successfully contested. When he was sworn in as prime minister after winning the leadership election, Turner was not an MP or senator — the last time this would occur until [Mark Carney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Carney "Mark Carney") in [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Liberal_Party_of_Canada_leadership_election "2025 Liberal Party of Canada leadership election"). Turner held the office of prime minister for just 79 days,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-1) as he advised the [governor general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_General_of_Canada "Governor General of Canada") to [dissolve Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_parliament "Dissolution of parliament") soon after being sworn in. He went on to lose the [1984 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Canadian_federal_election "1984 Canadian federal election") in a landslide to [Brian Mulroney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Mulroney "Brian Mulroney")'s [Progressive Conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Conservative_Party_of_Canada "Progressive Conservative Party of Canada"), leading the Liberals to the second-worst defeat for a governing party at the federal level (in terms of proportion of seats). Reentering parliament as the member for [Vancouver Quadra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver_Quadra "Vancouver Quadra"), Turner stayed on as Liberal leader and led the Opposition for the next six years.

In the [1988 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Canadian_federal_election "1988 Canadian federal election"), Turner vigorously campaigned against Mulroney's [proposed free trade agreement with the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada%E2%80%93United_States_Free_Trade_Agreement "Canada–United States Free Trade Agreement"), and led the Liberals to a modest recovery. He resigned as party leader in [1990](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Liberal_Party_of_Canada_leadership_election "1990 Liberal Party of Canada leadership election"), and did not seek re-election as an MP in [1993](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_Canadian_federal_election "1993 Canadian federal election").

Turner was Canada's first prime minister born in the United Kingdom since [Mackenzie Bowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mackenzie_Bowell "Mackenzie Bowell") in 1896, Canada's second shortest-serving prime minister behind [Charles Tupper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Tupper "Charles Tupper"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-Butler-2) and Canada's fifth longest-lived prime minister, living to the age of 91.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Turner was born on June 7, 1929,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-Bothwell_CanadianEncyclopedia-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-nyt1984-4) in [Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond,_London "Richmond, London"), [Surrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrey "Surrey"), England (now a part of London), to Leonard Hugh Turner, an English journalist with _[The Manchester Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Manchester\_Guardian "The Manchester Guardian")_,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-nyt1984-4) and [Phyllis Gregory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phyllis_Ross "Phyllis Ross"), a Canadian economist.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-5) He had a brother, Michael, born in 1930 (who died shortly after birth), and a sister, Brenda, born in 1931.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-cbcarchives-6) When Turner's father died in 1932, he and his sister moved to Canada with their Canadian-born mother. The family settled in her childhood home in [Rossland, British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rossland,_British_Columbia "Rossland, British Columbia"), and later moved to [Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa "Ottawa").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-nyt1984-4)

Turner's mother was loving but demanding of her two children.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-cbcarchives-6) The family was not wealthy.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-nyt1984-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-cbcarchives-6) His mother remarried in 1945 to [Frank Mackenzie Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Mackenzie_Ross "Frank Mackenzie Ross"), who later served as [Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_Governor_of_British_Columbia "Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia"), and the family relocated to [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-highlights-7)

### Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Education")]

Turner was educated at [Ashbury College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashbury_College "Ashbury College") and St Patrick's College, Ottawa (senior matriculation). He enrolled at the [University of British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_British_Columbia "University of British Columbia") (UBC) in 1945 at age 16 where he was a member of the UBC chapter of the [Beta Theta Pi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_Theta_Pi "Beta Theta Pi") fraternity, and was among Canada's outstanding track sprinters in the late 1940s.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-10) He held the Canadian record for the men's [100-yard dash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/100-yard_dash "100-yard dash") and qualified for the [1948 London Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_London_Olympics "1948 London Olympics"), but a bad knee kept him from competing.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-JAllemang_2009-06-05-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-12) He graduated from UBC with a BA (Honours) in 1949.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-highlights-7)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-:0-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-14)

Awarded a [Rhodes Scholarship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_Scholarship "Rhodes Scholarship"), Turner went on to [Magdalen College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalen_College,_Oxford "Magdalen College, Oxford") at the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford"), where he earned a BA in [jurisprudence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurisprudence "Jurisprudence") in 1951, and a [BCL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Civil_Law "Bachelor of Civil Law") in 1952; his BA was promoted to an [MA per tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Arts_(Oxford,_Cambridge,_and_Dublin) "Master of Arts (Oxford, Cambridge, and Dublin)") in 1957.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] He was on the track and field team at Oxford. One of his teammates was [Roger Bannister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Bannister "Roger Bannister"), who became the first runner to break the four-minute barrier in the mile.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-JAllemang_2009-06-05-11) At Oxford, Turner was a classmate and friend of future Australian prime ministers [Malcolm Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Fraser "Malcolm Fraser") and [Bob Hawke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Hawke "Bob Hawke"), as well as [Jeremy Thorpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Thorpe "Jeremy Thorpe"), future leader of Britain's [Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_(UK) "Liberal Party (UK)").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-darling-16) He also pursued doctoral studies at the [University of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Paris "University of Paris") from 1952 to 1953.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-highlights-7)

### Relationship with Princess Margaret

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Relationship with Princess Margaret")]

On July 25, 1958, a ball was hosted by Turner's mother and stepfather (in the latter's role of Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia), in honour of Princess Margaret at [HMCS Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMCS_Discovery "HMCS Discovery"), the Royal Canadian Navy's reserve station in [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver"). Turner danced with [Princess Margaret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Margaret,_Countess_of_Snowdon "Princess Margaret, Countess of Snowdon"),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-17) one year his junior, and they sat out talking, refusing requests to return to supper. This was the first time that Turner received significant press attention in Canada. Further meetings between them during Margaret's three week official visit to Canada led to considerable speculation about whether the two would become a serious couple. Contemporary press reports suggested there was some consternation about the reports among British officials, but their Canadian counterparts were more relaxed.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-18)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-cbcarchives-6)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-StarDelacourt-19)

A year later, in September 1959, press attention returned when reports circulated that Turner had been a recent guest at Balmoral in August where discussions had taken place concerning marriage between the pair; that he had also paid a secret visit to see her in April and that his parents had commented on their close friendship during their visit to Scotland in August.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-20)

According to letters discovered in 2015, written by Margaret to her friend Sharman Douglas and obtained by the _[Daily Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Mail "Daily Mail")_, the relationship was more serious than previously thought with the princess writing in one letter, seven years later: "John Turner is here & we meet on Thursday. It will seem so funny as we haven't met since I nearly married him & he's bringing his wife!". Turner told the _Daily Mail_: "I have never talked about it, and I am not going to start talking about it now".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-21) Brenda confirmed a "very definite attraction" between her brother and the princess, but said that Turner was uninterested in royalty and would not have given up Catholicism.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-brewster-22)

It has been claimed Turner attended Margaret's party at [Balmoral Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balmoral_Castle "Balmoral Castle") in August 1959 where his roommate was Margaret's future husband [Antony Armstrong-Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antony_Armstrong-Jones "Antony Armstrong-Jones");[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-brewster-22) however, according to his authorized biography, Armstrong-Jones visited Balmoral for the first time in early October 1959.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-23) Turner was the only Canadian unofficial guest at [their wedding in May 1960](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedding_of_Princess_Margaret_and_Antony_Armstrong-Jones "Wedding of Princess Margaret and Antony Armstrong-Jones"). Turner remained friends with Margaret, he and his wife often meeting the princess in Britain or during official visits to Canada. They attended Margaret's 2002 private funeral and were Canada's official representatives at the memorial service.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-brewster-22)

### Marriage and family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Marriage and family")]

Turner was married on May 11, 1963, to [Geills McCrae Kilgour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geills_Turner "Geills Turner") (b. 1937) who was then a [systems engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_engineering "Systems engineering") with [IBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM"),[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-24) and the great niece of Canadian Army doctor [John McCrae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCrae "John McCrae"), the author of what is probably the best-known First World War poem, "[In Flanders Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Flanders_Fields "In Flanders Fields")", and sister of [David Kilgour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Kilgour "David Kilgour"), a long-time Canadian [Member of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(Canada) "Member of Parliament (Canada)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-nyt1984-4) The Turners had daughter named Elizabeth and three sons: Michael, David, and Andrew.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-darling-16) David died in 2021. The Turner children attended [Rockcliffe Park Public School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockcliffe_Park_Public_School "Rockcliffe Park Public School"), in [Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa "Ottawa").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-FOOTNOTELitt201117-25) All three sons attended [Upper Canada College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Canada_College "Upper Canada College"), in [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-26)

## Early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Early career")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Captain_Burdock_presnted_with_NORAD_award_Shield_of_Freedom.jpg/250px-Captain_Burdock_presnted_with_NORAD_award_Shield_of_Freedom.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Captain_Burdock_presnted_with_NORAD_award_Shield_of_Freedom.jpg)

Turner presents Captain Burdock with the NORAD _Shield of Freedom_ award, on [CCGS John Cabot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CCGS_John_Cabot "CCGS John Cabot") while it was docked at the [Port of Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Montreal "Port of Montreal")

Turner practised law, initially with the firm of [Stikeman Elliott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stikeman_Elliott "Stikeman Elliott") in [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal"), Quebec.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-27) He was elected as Member of [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Canada "Parliament of Canada") for [St. Lawrence—St. George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Lawrence%E2%80%94St._George "St. Lawrence—St. George") in 1962 and was reelected there in every election until the riding's dissolution in 1968. He was the Member of Parliament for [Ottawa—Carleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa%E2%80%94Carleton_(federal_electoral_district) "Ottawa—Carleton (federal electoral district)") from 1968 to 1976.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-:0-13)

In 1965, while vacationing in [Barbados](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbados "Barbados"), Turner noticed that former prime minister and [Leader of the Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Opposition_(Canada) "Leader of the Opposition (Canada)")[John Diefenbaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Diefenbaker "John Diefenbaker"), staying at the same hotel, was struggling in the strong [surf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_surface_wave "Ocean surface wave") and [undertow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undertow_(wave_action) "Undertow (wave action)"). Turner, a competitive swimmer while in university, jumped in and pulled Diefenbaker to shore.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-28)

## Cabinet minister

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Cabinet minister")]

Turner was generally respected for his work as a cabinet minister in the 1960s and 1970s, under prime ministers [Lester Pearson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Pearson "Lester Pearson") and [Pierre Trudeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau "Pierre Trudeau").

### Premiership of Lester Pearson

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Premiership of Lester Pearson")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Her_Majesty_Queen_Elizabeth_II_and_her_Canadian_Ministers_at_Rideau_Hall_1_July_1967.jpg/250px-Her_Majesty_Queen_Elizabeth_II_and_her_Canadian_Ministers_at_Rideau_Hall_1_July_1967.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Her_Majesty_Queen_Elizabeth_II_and_her_Canadian_Ministers_at_Rideau_Hall_1_July_1967.jpg)

Her Majesty [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_II "Queen Elizabeth II") and her Canadian Ministers at [Rideau Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rideau_Hall "Rideau Hall") for Canada Day July 1, 1967

Turner served in the [Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Canada "Cabinet of Canada") of Prime Minister [Lester Pearson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_B._Pearson "Lester B. Pearson") in various capacities, most notably as [Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Consumer_and_Corporate_Affairs "Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs"). When Pearson retired, Turner ran to succeed him at the [1968 leadership convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Liberal_Party_of_Canada_leadership_election "1968 Liberal Party of Canada leadership election"). Turner, at age 38 the youngest of the dozen leadership candidates, stated "My time is now",[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-29) and remarked during his speech that he was "not here for some vague, future convention in, say, [1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Liberal_Party_of_Canada_leadership_election "1984 Liberal Party of Canada leadership election")".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-30) Turner stayed on until the fourth and final ballot, finishing third behind [Pierre Trudeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau "Pierre Trudeau") and runner-up [Robert Winters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Winters "Robert Winters").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPenniman198870-31)

### Premiership of Pierre Trudeau

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Premiership of Pierre Trudeau")]

Turner served in Trudeau's cabinet as [minister of justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Justice_(Canada) "Minister of Justice (Canada)") for four years. Biographer Paul Litt argues that Turner was a hard-working, well-informed minister whose success was assured by his warm relationship with his peers. His achievements, say Litt, included strengthening the rights of individual defendants on trial, greater efficiency in the justice system, creation of the influential [Law Reform Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_Commission_of_Canada "Law Commission of Canada"), selecting highly professional judges, and bringing a policy perspective to the Justice Department. He led the government's position in the highly controversial [Official Languages Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Languages_Act_(Canada) "Official Languages Act (Canada)"), and he took control during the [October Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Crisis "October Crisis") in 1970.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-FOOTNOTELitt20115%E2%80%937-32)

A member of the [Business Liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Grit "Blue Grit") faction of the Liberal Party,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-33) Turner then served as [Minister of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Finance_(Canada) "Minister of Finance (Canada)") from 1972 until 1975. His challenges were severe in the face of global financial issues such as the [1973 oil crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis "1973 oil crisis"), the collapse of the postwar [Bretton Woods trading system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_system "Bretton Woods system"), slowing economic growth combined with soaring inflation ([stagflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stagflation "Stagflation")), and growing deficits.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-Butler-2)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-FOOTNOTELitt2011viii-34) His positions were more conservative than Trudeau's and they drew apart. In 1975 Turner surprisingly resigned from cabinet.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-Bothwell_CanadianEncyclopedia-3) The Liberals had won the [1974 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Canadian_federal_election "1974 Canadian federal election") by attacking [Robert Stanfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Stanfield "Robert Stanfield")'s [Progressive Conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Conservative_Party_of_Canada "Progressive Conservative Party of Canada") over their platform involving wage and price controls. However, Trudeau decided to implement the wage and price controls in late 1975. In a 2013 interview with [Catherine Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Clark_(broadcaster) "Catherine Clark (broadcaster)") on [CPAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CPAC_(TV_channel) "CPAC (TV channel)"), Turner confirmed his resignation from cabinet was a direct result of refusing to implement wage and price controls, after campaigning against them in 1974.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-35)

In his memoirs, Trudeau wrote that Turner said he resigned as Finance Minister in 1975 because he was tired of politics, after 13 years in Ottawa, and wanted to move on to a better-paying job as a lawyer in Toronto, to better support his family and to be with them more, as his children were growing up. Trudeau also suggested that Turner's years as finance minister were very difficult because of turbulent and unusual conditions in the world economy, characterized as [stagflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stagflation "Stagflation"), largely caused by enormous increases in the price of oil.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-36)

## Bay Street

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Bay Street")]

From 1975 to 1984, Turner worked as a corporate lawyer at the [Bay Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Street "Bay Street") law firm [McMillan Binch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McMillan_Binch_Mendelsohn_LLP "McMillan Binch Mendelsohn LLP").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-37) When Pierre Trudeau resigned as Liberal leader in 1979 following an [election loss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_Canadian_federal_election "1979 Canadian federal election"), Turner announced that he would not be a candidate for the Liberal leadership. Trudeau was talked into rescinding his resignation after the government of [Joe Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Clark "Joe Clark") was defeated by a [motion of no confidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_of_no_confidence "Motion of no confidence"), and returned to contest and win the [1980 federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Canadian_federal_election "1980 Canadian federal election"). Trudeau then served as Prime Minister until 1984.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-38)

## Prime Minister (June–September 1984)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Prime Minister (June–September 1984)")]

Trudeau retired after polls showed the Liberals faced certain defeat in the next election if he remained in office. Turner then re-entered politics, and defeated [Jean Chrétien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Chr%C3%A9tien "Jean Chrétien"), his successor as finance minister, on the second ballot of the [June 1984 Liberal leadership convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Liberal_Party_of_Canada_leadership_election "1984 Liberal Party of Canada leadership election"). He was formally appointed prime minister on June 30.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-darling-16) When he was sworn in, Turner was not an MP or senator; the next occurrence of a PM not being elected to the Commons or Senate would be [Mark Carney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Carney "Mark Carney") in [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Liberal_Party_of_Canada_leadership_election "2025 Liberal Party of Canada leadership election"). He also announced that he would not run in a by-election to get into the Commons, but would instead run in the next general election as the Liberal candidate in the [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia") riding of [Vancouver Quadra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver_Quadra "Vancouver Quadra"), a seat held by the Tories. This was part of Turner's strategy to rebuild the Liberals' image in [western Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Canada "Western Canada"); at the time, the party held no seats west of [Winnipeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnipeg "Winnipeg").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-39)

In his final days of office, Trudeau recommended that [Governor General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_General_of_Canada "Governor General of Canada")[Jeanne Sauvé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Sauv%C3%A9 "Jeanne Sauvé") appoint over 200 Liberals to [patronage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage "Patronage") positions, including [senators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Canada "Senate of Canada"), judges, and executives on various governmental and [crown corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_corporation "Crown corporation") boards. Turner then made a further 19 appointments himself, one of Trudeau's conditions for retiring earlier than he had planned.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-Mulroney_1991-40)

### 1984 federal election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 1984 federal election")]

Main article: [1984 Canadian federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Canadian_federal_election "1984 Canadian federal election")

On July 9, only nine days after being sworn in, Turner asked Sauvé to dissolve parliament and advised her to [call an election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Canadian_federal_election "1984 Canadian federal election") for early September. Progressive Conservative leader Brian Mulroney and other experts had expected Turner to tour Canada during the summer and early autumn, accompanying [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_II "Queen Elizabeth II") and [Pope John Paul II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_Paul_II "Pope John Paul II") on their upcoming visits, and then call the election for later in the autumn.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-Mulroney_1991-40) As the campaign unfolded, the Tories and Mulroney, who was fighting his first general election in any capacity, soon took the lead.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-Mulroney_1991-40)

Early in the campaign, Turner appeared rusty and old-fashioned.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-FOOTNOTELitt2011237-41) His policies contrasted with Trudeau's and seemed to legitimize the Tory calls for lowering the deficit, improving relations with the United States, cutting the bureaucracy, and promoting more federal-provincial harmony. He spoke of creating "make work projects",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-Bothwell_CanadianEncyclopedia-3) a discarded phrase from the 1970s that had been replaced by the less patronizing "[job creation programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Job_creation_program "Job creation program")". Turner was also caught on television patting the bottoms of Liberal Party President [Iona Campagnolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iona_Campagnolo "Iona Campagnolo") and Vice-President Lise St. Martin-Tremblay, causing an uproar among [feminists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminists "Feminists"), who saw such behaviour as sexist and condescending.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-42)

During the televised leaders' debate, Turner attacked Mulroney over the patronage machine that the latter had allegedly set up in anticipation of victory, comparing it to the [Union Nationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Nationale_(Quebec) "Union Nationale (Quebec)") governments of [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec"). Mulroney responded by pointing to the raft of patronage appointments made on the advice of Trudeau and Turner. Turner had the right to advise Sauvé to cancel Trudeau's appointments—advice that she was bound to follow by convention—but failed to do so and added to his own. Mulroney demanded that Turner apologize to the country for what he called "these horrible appointments." Turner claimed that "I had no option" except to let them stand. Mulroney responded, "[You had an option, sir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_had_an_option,_sir "You had an option, sir")–to say 'no'–and you chose to say 'yes' to the old attitudes and the old stories of the Liberal Party." He highlighted the Liberals' long record in government and resulting patronage appointments.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-43)

Turner discovered late in the campaign that the Liberals' electoral hopes were poor in their traditional stronghold of Quebec.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-44) The party had heretofore relied on Trudeau's appeal, patronage, and traditional dislike of the Progressive Conservatives for victory in recent previous elections. Turner had surrounded himself with Trudeau's factional opponents and Trudeau himself did not endorse Turner.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPenniman1988106%E2%80%9313-45) In a last-minute turnaround, Turner rehired much of Trudeau's staff during the final weeks, but this had little effect. Quebec's disaffection with the federal Liberals regarding [patriation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriation "Patriation") in 1982 further contributed to their defeat. Mulroney, a native [Quebecker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Quebec "Demographics of Quebec"), was able to harness that discontent to the Progressive Conservatives' advantage by promising a new constitutional agreement.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-Mulroney_1991-40)

On September 4, the Liberals were swept from power in a Tory landslide.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPenniman198837-46) The Liberals were cut down to 40 seats, the fewest in the party's history until [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Federal_Election_2011 "Canadian Federal Election 2011"), against 211 for the Progressive Conservatives. The Liberals fell to 17 seats in Quebec, all but four in and around [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal"). Eleven members of Turner's cabinet were defeated. It was the worst defeat the Liberals experienced in a federal election since [1958](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1958_Canadian_federal_election "1958 Canadian federal election").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPenniman198837-46)

Turner stepped down as prime minister on September 17.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-47) The election having been called just over a week after his being sworn in, Turner held the office of prime minister for two months and seventeen days, the second-shortest stint in Canadian history, ahead of only [Sir Charles Tupper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Tupper "Charles Tupper"), who took office after dissolution of parliament.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-FOOTNOTELitt2011290-48) Turner, along with Tupper and later Mulroney's successor, [Kim Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Campbell "Kim Campbell"), were the only PMs who never faced a parliament or implemented any legislative initiative.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-49)

## Opposition leader (1984–1990)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Opposition leader (1984–1990)")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Ronald_Reagan_and_John_Turner_1987_crop.jpg/250px-Ronald_Reagan_and_John_Turner_1987_crop.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ronald_Reagan_and_John_Turner_1987_crop.jpg)

Turner with President [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") at [Rideau Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rideau_Hall "Rideau Hall"), April 1987.

In 1984, Turner managed to defeat the Tory incumbent in Vancouver Quadra, Bill Clarke by 3,200 votes, a surprising result given the size of the Tory wave, and became [leader of the opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Opposition_(Canada) "Leader of the Opposition (Canada)").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-50) He was the only Liberal MP from British Columbia, and one of only two from west of Ontario. The Liberals, amid their worst showing in party history and led by an unpopular Turner, were said by some pundits to be following the [British Liberals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_(UK) "Liberal Party (UK)") into oblivion. Though the Liberals had not fared much better in the [1958 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1958_Canadian_federal_election "1958 Canadian federal election"), they had clearly emerged as the main opposition party back then. After the [1984 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Canadian_federal_election "1984 Canadian federal election"), however, the NDP were not far behind with 30 seats.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-51) Their leader [Ed Broadbent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Broadbent "Ed Broadbent") consistently outpolled Turner and even Mulroney, except in Quebec.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-52)

The Liberals responded by using their large [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Canada "Senate of Canada") majority, built up over years of Liberal majorities in the Commons, to stall Mulroney's legislation. In addition, a group of young Liberal MPs, known as the "[Rat Pack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_of_Canada_Rat_Pack "Liberal Party of Canada Rat Pack")", pestered Mulroney at every turn. The group included [Sheila Copps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheila_Copps "Sheila Copps"), [Brian Tobin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Tobin "Brian Tobin"), [Don Boudria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Boudria "Don Boudria"), and [John Nunziata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Nunziata "John Nunziata").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-53)

Turner's leadership was frequently questioned, and in the lead up to the 1986 Liberal convention, a vote of confidence loomed large. The popular Jean Chrétien resigned his seat, creating a stir in caucus. [Keith Davey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Davey "Keith Davey") publicly voiced his concerns with Turner's leadership,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-54) which coincided with backroom struggles involving Chrétien's supporters. The public conflict is said to have influenced many Liberals to support Turner, and he ended up getting a little over 75% of the delegate vote.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-55) The Liberals faced more internal conflict in the next few years, but polls frequently had them in front of the Progressive Conservatives (but with Turner last in preferred prime minister categories). The upcoming [Canada–US Free Trade Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada%E2%80%93US_Free_Trade_Agreement "Canada–US Free Trade Agreement") (FTA) and [Meech Lake Accord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meech_Lake_Accord "Meech Lake Accord") threatened to divide the party until Turner took the position of being pro-Meech Lake[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-56) and against the FTA. Turner asked the Liberal Senators to hold off on passing the legislation to implement the agreement until an election was held. It was later revealed that Mulroney planned to have an election called, anyway.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-57)

### 1988 federal election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: 1988 federal election")]

Main article: [1988 Canadian federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Canadian_federal_election "1988 Canadian federal election")

When the [election was called for November 21, 1988](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Canadian_federal_election "1988 Canadian federal election"), the Liberals had some early struggles, notably during one day in Montreal where 3 different costs were given for the proposed Liberal daycare program. The campaign was also hampered by a [Canadian Broadcasting Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Broadcasting_Corporation "Canadian Broadcasting Corporation") report that stated there was a movement in the backroom to replace Turner with Chrétien.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-:1-59)

Turner campaigned rallying support against the proposed FTA, an agreement that he said would lead to the abandonment of Canada's political sovereignty to the United States.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-FOOTNOTELitt2011-61) His performance in the debate and his attacks on Mulroney and the FTA, where he accused the Progressive Conservative Prime Minister of selling Canada out with one signature of a pen,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-:1-59) raised his poll numbers, and soon the Liberals were hoping for a majority. This prompted the Progressive Conservatives to stop the relatively calm campaign they had been running, and follow [Allan Gregg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Gregg "Allan Gregg")'s suggestion of "bombing the bridge" that joined anti-FTA voters and the Liberals, Turner's credibility.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-62) The ads focused on Turner's leadership struggles, and combined with over $6 million in pro-FTA ads, stopped Turner's momentum. Also not helping the Liberals was that the NDP had opposed the FTA as well (though not as vocally); this likely resulted in vote-splitting between the opposition parties. Although most Canadians voted for parties opposed to [free trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_trade "Free trade"), the Tories were returned with a majority government, and implemented the deal.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-auto-63)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-darling-16)

The Liberals more than doubled their representation to 83 seats, and kept their role as the [Official Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Opposition_(Canada) "Official Opposition (Canada)"); the NDP had also made gains but finished a distant third with 43 seats. The Progressive Conservatives won a reduced majority government with 169 seats.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-:1-59)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-auto-63)

The election loss seemed to confirm Turner's fate; he announced he was standing down from the party leadership in May 1989,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-64) officially resigning in June 1990. Turner resigned as Official Opposition leader, while still holding the Liberal leadership, so [Herb Gray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Gray "Herb Gray") became the [caucus leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_leader "Parliamentary leader") in the interim.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-65) Chrétien won that year's [leadership convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Liberal_Party_of_Canada_leadership_election "1990 Liberal Party of Canada leadership election") over [Paul Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Martin "Paul Martin").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-66) Although not officially endorsed by Turner himself, Martin was widely the favourite of Turner's supporters.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-67)

Turner continued to represent Vancouver Quadra in the House of Commons before retiring from politics in the 1993 election.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-:0-13)

## After politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: After politics")]

In 1990, Turner returned to practising law, this time working for Miller Thomson LLP, while he continued serving as an MP for another three years. He eventually became head of the firm's scholarship program. Turner was also a board member for several corporations.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-Bothwell_CanadianEncyclopedia-3)

Turner was a member of the Canadian delegation that monitored the runoff vote in the [2004 Ukrainian presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Ukrainian_presidential_election "2004 Ukrainian presidential election").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-Bothwell_CanadianEncyclopedia-3)

Turner voiced his support for the [Campaign for the Establishment of a United Nations Parliamentary Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_for_the_Establishment_of_a_United_Nations_Parliamentary_Assembly "Campaign for the Establishment of a United Nations Parliamentary Assembly"), an organization which campaigns for democratic reformation of the United Nations, and the creation of a more accountable international political system.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-68)

In 2017, he was awarded the Gold Medal of the [Royal Canadian Geographical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Geographical_Society "Royal Canadian Geographical Society").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-69) Turner lived in the [Deer Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deer_Park,_Toronto "Deer Park, Toronto") neighbourhood of Toronto.

## Death and state funeral

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Turner&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Death and state funeral")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Prime_Minister_John_Turner_gravesite_photo.jpg/250px-Prime_Minister_John_Turner_gravesite_photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prime_Minister_John_Turner_gravesite_photo.jpg)

Turner's grave site in Mount Pleasant Cemetery

Turner died on September 19, 2020, at age 91,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-CanadaHeritage_2020-09-22-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-73) from [congestive heart failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congestive_heart_failure "Congestive heart failure").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPaikin2022285-74) A [state funeral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_funerals_in_Canada "State funerals in Canada") was held for Turner on October 6, 2020, at [St. Michael's Cathedral Basilica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Michael's_Cathedral_Basilica_(Toronto) "St. Michael's Cathedral Basilica (Toronto)") in Toronto. The ceremony was scaled back due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Canada "COVID-19 pandemic in Canada") with masking and [social distancing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_distancing "Social distancing") protocols in place, attendance limited to 160 guests, with no [lying in state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lying_in_state "Lying in state").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-CanadaHeritage_2020-09-22-72)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-75) Turner was buried in a private service at [Mount Pleasant Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Pleasant_Cemetery,_Toronto "Mount Pleasant Cemetery, Toronto").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPaikin2022294-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-77) Turner and Mackenzie King are two former prime ministers interred at Mount Pleasant.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-78)

According to Canadian protocol, as a former prime minister, he was styled _[The Right Honourable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Right\_Honourable "The Right Honourable")_ for life.

Turner was ranked 18th out of the first 20 Prime Ministers of Canada (through [Jean Chrétien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Chr%C3%A9tien "Jean Chrétien")) by a survey of Canadian historians in 1999. The survey was used in the book _Prime Ministers: Ranking Canada's Leaders_ by [J. L. Granatstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._L._Granatstein "J. L. Granatstein") and [Norman Hillmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Hillmer "Norman Hillmer").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-85)

Turner was appointed a Companion of the [Order of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Canada "Order of Canada") on October 19, 1994, and was invested on May 3, 1995. His citation reads:

> He became Canada's seventeenth Prime Minister, crowning a distinguished parliamentary career during which he held several key Cabinet portfolios. Parallel to his political life, he has been a respected member of the law profession and supporter of many charitable organizations, in particular Mount Sinai Hospital and the Community Foundation of Toronto. His passion for his country is admired by all Canadians.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner#cite_note-86)
